speaker: king
opening: Heroes. You stand summoned in our darkest hour.
I shall be brief, for the matter is grave.
The sky above the northern marches has gone thin.
Thin as old vellum, and something reads through it.
Our astronomers call it the Unlidding.
They do not sleep any more. Nor, in truth, do I.
Rivers have begun to run a little uphill.
Bells ring at night in towns that own no bells.
The dead are not rising, but they are restless.
This is not weather. This is an ending.
It was foretold, and I must tell you how.
Nine hundred years ago a shepherd had a dream.
He dreamed eleven nights and woke with white hair.
His words were set down on the Tablet of Wend.
The Tablet is in three pieces. We possess two.
The first piece says: when the sky wears thin,
four shall come who were not sent for by name.
The second piece says: they shall mend the seals.
The third piece is believed to contain a warning.
We have searched for it for six generations.
I mention this so that you are fully informed.
You are the four. The reckoning admits no other.
My astrologers checked it twice, and then again.
Now attend, for I come to the seals.
There are seven seals, and each binds one silence.
The Seal of Ash lies beneath the old foundry.
The Seal of Brine sleeps under the salt harbor.
The Seal of Thorn is kept by an order of nuns.
The Seal of Glass was lost in the year of floods.
The Seal of Bone is not spoken of at table.
The Seal of Echo answers only a true question.
The seventh seal has no name. That is its name.
Three are cracked. One weeps. One is merely warm.
Each must be mended in its proper season.
And in its proper order, which is not this order.
The proper order is in the Canticle of Locks.
The Canticle has four hundred verses. I know them.
I will not recite them now. Perhaps a few.
First, hear the duties of the chosen.
The chosen shall rise before the sun on a seal day.
The chosen shall carry no iron to a seal chamber.
The chosen shall eat no quince until midwinter.
The chosen shall speak the Low Oath and the High.
The Low Oath is brief. It runs to some forty lines.
The High Oath is learned from a living keeper.
There is one living keeper. She is very old.
She dwells past the Marrow Hills. She dislikes guests.
You will bring her a gift of pears. It is custom.
The chosen shall tally every door they open.
The tally is rendered to the crown each quarter.
Forms for the tally are kept by my chamberlain.
These duties are no burden. They are an honor.
My own grandfather wept that he was not chosen.
Which brings me, rightly, to my grandfather.
He was Aldemar the Patient, ninth of our house.
Our house descends unbroken from Queen Isaude.
Unbroken, I say, though some scholars cite a cousin.
The cousin was legitimate. I have seen the papers.
Isaude begat Corwin, who built the first granary.
Corwin begat Merewen, who lost it in a wager.
Merewen begat twins. Here the record is delicate.
The elder twin, Hale, was elder by a single breath.
The younger, Hob, disputed that breath forty years.
From Hale, the crown. From Hob, the dukes of Orrin.
The dukes of Orrin have never forgotten the breath.
You will meet them. Do not raise the subject.
To settle the breath, the Accord was signed.
It is called the Accord of the Long Table.
Its first article sets the border at the river Senn.
Its second article concerns the river when it moves.
For the Senn does move. It moved in my father's time.
Its third article grants Orrin the tolls of a bridge.
The bridge has since fallen. The tolls are still owed.
This is a matter of principle on both sides.
A lesser accord governs the gathering of reeds.
I mention the reeds because a seal lies near them.
You see how everything touches upon the seals.
On my mother's side the matter is simpler.
She brought to the crown three valleys and a mill.
The mill came with a miller, by an old entailment.
His descendants hold the post to this day.
The present miller is the eleventh. A thoughtful man.
The valleys passed to me, and the mill to my sister.
My sister and I are on excellent terms.
We write each spring concerning the mill.
The valleys are given chiefly to barley.
Barley and, in the wetter fields, a blue-eared rye.
The rye was my great-uncle's notion. It has answered.
A field wants rest every third year. This is known.
Less known is what to sow in the resting year.
I favor clover. My steward favors vetch.
We have each kept figures on it for nineteen years.
The figures incline, I believe, toward clover.
I raise this because the seals affect the frost.
A cracked seal brings the frost early by nine days.
Nine days, heroes. Consider what that does to barley.
When you go before the keepers, go correctly.
One bows to a keeper from the waist, never the neck.
One does not offer the left hand in the Marrow Hills.
At an Orrin table the salt passes against the sun.
Should you be offered a third cup, decline it twice.
Accept it on the third offer, and drink but half.
A nun of the Thorn is addressed as Patience.
All of them. It is less confusing than it sounds.
Remove your hats before any seal. Also your spurs.
These are small things. A realm is made of them.
And so we return, as we must, to the seals.
I said that three are cracked. I shall say which.
Ash is cracked. Brine is cracked. Echo is cracked.
Glass weeps. Bone is warm. Thorn holds, for now.
Of the seventh we know only that it is listening.
When the last seal fails, the Unlidding is complete.
What comes through, the Tablet does not say.
Or rather, it says so on the piece we lack.
You understand, then, the weight of what I ask.
I do not ask it lightly. I have asked few before.
Before you set out, there is the matter of roads.
The realm has four great roads and a lesser fifth.
To explain the roads, I must say who built them.
To say who built them, I return to Queen Isaude.
For the line of Isaude is the line of the roads.
I shall give it in full, so that nothing is lost.

won it back by a marriage
matters: the weight of a lawful loaf
the width of a cart axle
